KISHKINDHA KANDA 
CHAPTER 3 
Hanuman's Meeting with Rama 
AT the command of the magnanimous Sugriva, Hanuman, 
with one bound, left the Mountain Rishyamuka and placed 
himself in the path of the two Raghavas. 
Discarding his monkey form, Hanuman, the son of Masuta, 
by the power of illusion, assumed the guise of a wandering 
monk and, in gentle and pleasing tones, addressed those two 
brothers with humility, paying obeisance to them. 
Approaching those two heroes, that Foremost of Monkeys 
praised them as they deserved, offering them every courtesy 
and in accord with Sugriva's wish spoke graciously to them, 
saying:-
" 0 Ascetics of renowned penance, who are full of faith and 
valour and who resemble the Rishis and the Gods, why have 
you come to this region, sowing fear amongst the herds of deer 
and other denizens of the forest, surveying the trees on every 
side that grow on the borders of Pampa, that lake of sparkling 
waves, the splendour of which you enhance with your radiance, 
0 Heroes of Great Daring ? 
" 0 Valiant Strangers, who are you, whose skin gleams like 
gold and who are clad in robes of bark, possessing strong arms, 
you who are sighing deeply and whose sight inspires fear in all 
beings ? You have the air of lions or warriors who are full of 
courage and heroism, armed as you are with bows, resembling 
lndra's, the Destroyers of your Foes ? 
"Full of majesty and beauty, mighty as great bulls, your 
arms resembling the trunks of elephanrs, radiant, the first 
among men, youthful, illumining the king of the mounrains with 
your effulgence, you who are worthy of ruling kingdoms and 
like unto the Gods, what purpose brings you here ? 0 Heroes, 
whose eyes are as large as lotus petals, who wear your matted 
locks coiled like crowns on your heads, who resemble each

0 Broad-chested Warriors, ye who are men, yet have 
the aspect of divine beings, whose shoulders are like unto a

bulls intoxicated with desire, whose large and massive arms 
look like clubs that should be adorned with every kind of

beautiful are your two shining bows, glistening with perfumed 
paste, covered with gold and shining like the mace of Indra ; 
the two quivers also, filled with sharp death-dealiog and 
formidable arrows resembling hissing snakes ; 
your two 
swords of immense length and size, encrusted with fine gold 
that gleam like serpents that have just cast their slough ! But 
why do ye not answer me ? 
" Sugriva is the name of that virtuous King of the Monkeys, 
that hero banished by his brother, who roams the earth in 
great distress. I have come here under the orders of that 
magnanimous one, the Chief of the Great Monkeys. 
The 
illustrious Sugriva desires your friendship. 
Know me to be 
his minister, a monkey, the son of Pavana, ranging where I 
please and coming here under the guise of a wandering monk 
from the Rishyamuka Mountain in order to please him." 
Having addressed those two heroes, Rama and Lakshmana, 
in discreet and courteous terms, Hanuman fell silent and hearing 
that speech, the blessed Rama, delighted, addressed Lakshmana 
who stood beside him, saying :-
" This is the minister of the King of the Monkeys, the 
magnanimous Sugriva, whom I seek. 
0 Saumitri, answer 
Sugriva's counsellor who is eloquent and warm-hearted and 
the subduer of his foes in courteous terms.

brief.summary_1line: Hanuman, disguised as a monk, approaches Rama and Lakshmana, praises them, and introduces himself as Sugriva’s minister seeking their friendship.

image_candidates.scene_text: Hanuman in the guise of a wandering monk stands before Rama and Lakshmana beside Lake Pampa, bowing respectfully as the princes hold their bows.
Rama and Lakshmana, radiant and armed with golden bows and quivers, stand like twin lions in the forest while the disguised Hanuman addresses them.
Rama turns to Lakshmana with a pleased expression, praising the eloquence of the humble monk who is secretly Hanuman.

deep.rich_summary: Sugriva sends his minister Hanuman to investigate two mysterious warriors approaching the region of Pampa near Mount Rishyamuka. Leaping down from the mountain, Hanuman disguises himself as a wandering ascetic and respectfully approaches the strangers—Rama and Lakshmana. Speaking with remarkable eloquence, he questions who they are, marveling at their divine appearance, their golden complexions, mighty arms, and formidable weapons. He suggests they seem almost celestial, like the sun and moon descended to earth. Hanuman then reveals his mission: he serves Sugriva, the exiled monkey king who seeks friendship with them. After hearing the speech, Rama is deeply impressed, telling Lakshmana that only someone thoroughly learned in the Vedas and grammar could speak so flawlessly. This moment marks the first meeting between Rama and Hanuman, initiating one of the epic’s most important alliances.

highlight_spans.why: The opening action—Hanuman leaping from Rishyamuka at Sugriva’s command—sets up the pivotal first encounter between Hanuman and Rama.
Hanuman disguises himself as a wandering monk and approaches with humility, highlighting his intelligence, diplomacy, and mastery of illusion.
Hanuman’s awestruck description of the brothers—comparing them to divine beings like the sun and moon—captures the reverence and wonder of the meeting.
Hanuman reveals Sugriva’s identity and mission, formally proposing friendship—this is the turning point that begins the Rama–Sugriva alliance.
Rama praises Hanuman’s flawless speech and learning in the Vedas, recognizing his wisdom and greatness at their very first meeting.

top_scenes.scene_text: Hanuman leaps from Mount Rishyamuka and lands before Rama and Lakshmana, then transforms into the calm form of a wandering ascetic to approach them.
Disguised as a monk, Hanuman stands before the radiant Rama and Lakshmana near the sparkling lake of Pampa, marveling at their divine warrior presence and golden bows.
Rama quietly tells Lakshmana that only a master of the Vedas could speak with such flawless eloquence as the mysterious messenger before them.
